title: Ruby preset content
description: content.json inside a preset container: a layer-stack fragment. Deliberately the SAME layer shape a .rbypr project uses, so there is one layer serialization and one parser rather than two that drift. A preset is a subtree of layers, not a single effect chain: a shake is a null plus expressions plus effects, a transition is several layers with time offsets and an SFX. Sapphire's own preset library measures this out, with a median of four chained components per preset and 40% using five or more.

layers.description: Topmost first, matching the timeline. Layer ids are local to the fragment and are remapped on apply.

media.description: Assets the fragment brings with it, by content-hashed path inside the container.

parent.description: Another layer id in this fragment.

effect.description: An effect id from D1. Immortal.

schema.description: The version this content was authored against. Loading it into a newer effect runs that effect's migration chain.

masks.description: Where this effect applies. Framework-level, so every effect takes them without knowing they exist.

shape.description: Refused if unknown, never guessed: a newer shape read as a rectangle would silently change what the effect covers.

unit.description: Why a preset authored on 1080x1920 lands correctly on 1920x1080. An unknown unit is refused, never defaulted: reading it as `normalized` would silently reinterpret every stored value.

value.description: Scalar or array, matching the parameter's component count.

property.description: No `range` key, on purpose. Limits belong to the effect's schema, not to saved content: a file that pinned its own would freeze them, so widening a range later would leave every existing preset on the old one with no way to tell.

time.description: A time authored in beats stays in beats. That is what makes a preset survive being dropped on a song at a different tempo, and it is why `frames` is opt-in rather than the default.
